## Introduction

How well does a fitted model predict data that were not used to fit it? The
formula reference (Vehtari et al., 2026) divides this into three questions:
<!-- TODO -->

1. **What counts as a good prediction?** This is the *predictive measure*, for
   example the log score or the RMSE.
   + Discussed in the vignette [Predictive model performance: Overview of measures](overview-measures.html)
2. **Which predictions are evaluated?** This is the *predictive scheme*. It
   sets the observations that train the model before observation $i$ is
   evaluated.
   + Focus of this vignette.
3. **How are the predictions computed?** From posterior draws, from refits, or
   with importance weights.

::: {.callout .callout-note}
**What this article does not cover**

+ **Measure definitions**
  + See the [Predictive model performance: Overview of measures](overview-measures.html).
+ **Model comparison** 
  + See the [Model comparison: Explanation of `model_compare()`](model-comparison.html)
  vignette and
  + the [Model comparison case study: Uncertainty, scores, and predictive schemes](pred-measure-case-study.html) <!-- TODO -->
+ **Leave-one-group-out and leave-future-out schemes.**
  + Any reference? <!-- TODO -->
:::

### Training data and evaluation data {#data-sets}

This vignette focuses on the predictive scheme. A predictive scheme is a rule
that splits the observed data $y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)$ into a training set
$\mathcal{T}$ used to fit the model and an evaluation set $\mathcal{E}$ (i.e., 
the observations whose predictive performance is evaluated).

For example, in the case of in-sample evaluation, the training set is the full
data set. In a hold-out evaluation, the data set is split into two disjoint
sets: one for training and one for evaluation.
Between these two extremes are cross-validation schemes, where the training
set is a subset of the data, and the evaluation set is the remaining data.
For example, in leave-one-out cross-validation, the training set is the full
data set minus one observation. In K-fold cross-validation, the training set is
the full data set minus one of $K$ disjoint subsets of the data (i.e., the folds).

### Overview of the predictive schemes

The predictive measure API in the **loo** package has one entry point for
each predictive scheme:

| Scheme | Training data $\mathcal{T}(i)$ | Evaluation data $\mathcal{E}$ | Predictive distribution $p^q(y_i)$ | Weights $w_i^s$ | Entry point |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [in-sample](#in-sample) | $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ | $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ | $p(y_i \mid y)$ | $1/S$ | `insample_pred_measure()` |
| [LOO](#psis-loo)* | $\{1, \ldots, n\} \setminus \{i\}$ | $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ | $p(y_i \mid y_{-i})$ | PSIS weights | `loo_pred_measure()` |
| [K-fold](#k-fold) | $\{1, \ldots, n\} \setminus \mathcal{I}_{k(i)}$ | $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ | $p(y_i \mid y_{-\mathcal{I}_{k(i)}})$ | $1/S$ | `kfold_pred_measure()` |
| [test data](#test-data) | $\mathcal{R}$ | $\mathcal{S}$ | $p(y_i \mid y_{\mathcal{R}})$ | $1/S$ | `test_pred_measure()` |

*here with focus on PSIS-LOO.

For further discussion, see the paper [Predictive measures: A formula reference]() <!-- TODO -->.

## Running example

**Prediction task.** The `sleepstudy` data (**lme4**) come from a study of sleep
restriction (Belenky et al., 2003). Eighteen subjects slept at most three hours
each night. The outcome `y` is the average reaction time (ms) of a subject on
one day. Days 0 and 1 were adaptation and training, so this vignette keeps days
2 to 9. The predictor `Days` counts the days of sleep restriction, from 0 to 7.
This gives 144 observations.

```{r load-libraries-internal, echo=FALSE}
devtools::load_all("../..", quiet = TRUE)
devtools::load_all("../../../../GitHub/brms", quiet = TRUE)
library(ggplot2)

theme_set(theme_minimal())
SEED <- 42
```

```{r load-libraries, eval=FALSE}
library(loo)      # for evaluating the predictive performance
library(brms)     # for model fitting
library(lme4)     # for the sleepstudy data
library(ggplot2)  # for plotting

theme_set(theme_minimal())
SEED <- 42
```

The model is a normal regression of `y` on `Days`. It has no subject effects.
As fitting is not the focus of this vignette, we do not discuss the modelling
step in depth but show the code in the [appendix](#appendix-model-code).

| Object | Data | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `fit_full` | all 18 subjects, 144 observations | fit to full data|
| `fit_train` | 13 subjects, 104 observations | fit to training data |
| `test_data` | the other 5 subjects, 40 observations | test data set |

Each fit uses the `brms` default of 4 chains and 2000 iterations.

```{r fit-models, echo=FALSE, results="hide"}
set.seed(SEED)

data("sleepstudy", package = "lme4")
sleepstudy <- subset(sleepstudy, Days >= 2)
sleepstudy$Days <- sleepstudy$Days - 2
sleepstudy$y <- sleepstudy$Reaction

prior_sleep <- brms::prior(normal(200, 100), class = b, coef = "Intercept") +
  brms::prior(normal(0, 20), class = b, coef = "Days") +
  brms::prior(exponential(0.02), class = sigma)

# all subjects
fit_full <- brms::brm(
  y ~ 0 + Intercept + Days,
  data = sleepstudy,
  family = gaussian(),
  prior = prior_sleep,
  seed = SEED,
  refresh = 0
)

# five subjects held out as test data
test_subjects <- sample(unique(sleepstudy$Subject), size = 5)
train_data <- subset(sleepstudy, !Subject %in% test_subjects)
test_data <- subset(sleepstudy, Subject %in% test_subjects)

fit_train <- update(
  fit_full, newdata = train_data, seed = SEED, refresh = 0
)
```

### Measures

For the example, we will use the following measures to evaluate the 
predictive performance of the model: `elpd`, `mlpd`, `rps`, `rmse`, and `r2`.
See the vignette [Predictive model performance: Overview of measures](overview-measures.html)
for a discussion of the measures.

Each measure requires specific inputs: the observed values (`y`), the
pointwise log predictive densities (`ylp`), the predicted means (`mupred`),
or draws from the predictive distribution (`ypred`). The following table
summarizes the input requirements for the measures used in this example.

| Measure | `y` | `ylp` | `mupred` | `ypred` |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `elpd` | | ✓ | | |
| `mlpd` | | ✓ | | |
| `rps` | ✓ | | | ✓ |
| `rmse` | ✓ | | ✓ | |
| `r2` | ✓ | | ✓ | |

```{r inputs}
measures <- c("elpd", "mlpd", "rps", "rmse", "r2")

y <- fit_full$data$y
ylp <- brms::log_lik(fit_full)
ypred <- brms::posterior_predict(fit_full)
mupred <- brms::posterior_epred(fit_full)
```

## Predictive schemes
### In-sample {#in-sample}
We start the discussion with the special case of using in-sample evaluations.
In-sample performance evaluates the fitted model on the same data used for
fitting and is therefore typically optimistic as an estimate of performance
on new data. Thus, it should not be used to estimate predictive performance.
Nevertheless, it can be useful as a reference point, and the amount of optimism
relative to a cross-validation or test-data estimate can itself be informative.

**Implementation**

```{r insample}
insample_sleep <- insample_pred_measure(
  y = y,
  ypred = ypred,
  mupred = mupred,
  ylp = ylp,
  measures = measures
)
str(insample_sleep)
```

**Result**
The returned structure of the `pred_measure` class includes the
`$estimates` and `$pointwise` components per selected measure. Furthermore, the
following attributes are included in the result:

+ `measure_info`: a list with entries for each measure with respective additional information
+ `source`: indicates the predictive scheme used, here `"insample"`.
+ `dims`: provides the dimensions of the data used for evaluation.
+ `class`: indicates the class of the result, here `"pred_measure"` and `"insample_pred_measure"`.

The corresponding print method shows the estimates and standard errors for
each measure, as well as the number of observations used for evaluation.

```{r insample-print}
insample_sleep
```

### PSIS-LOO {#psis-loo}
Next, we focus on the leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) scheme, specifically
using Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) to approximate the LOO
predictive performance. In this scheme, each observation is left out of the
training set one at a time.

While exact leave-one-out cross-validation needs one refit for each observation,
PSIS-LOO uses the draws of the full-data fit instead.
It gives them Pareto-smoothed importance weights, so that each $y_i$ is scored
as if it was left out (Vehtari et al., 2024).

**Implementation**
We first compute the PSIS-LOO object using `brms::loo()` and then pass it to
`loo_pred_measure()`. Otherwise, the input structure is the same as for the
in-sample evaluation.

```{r loo}
loo_sleep <- brms::loo(fit_full, save_psis = TRUE)

loo_sleep_measure <- loo_pred_measure(
  loo = loo_sleep,
  y = y,
  ypred = ypred,
  mupred = mupred,
  measures = measures
)
loo_sleep_measure
```

**Result**
Compared to the in-sample evaluation, the rows now have the suffix `_loo`.
The measure `elpd` also adds `p_loo`, the difference between the in-sample and
the LOO log score (Vehtari et al., 2026). <!-- TODO -->

The output structure of the `loo_pred_measure` class includes two additional
components compared to the `insample_pred_measure` class:

+ `$diagnostics`: including `pareto_k`, the Pareto $\hat k$ values for each
observation, and (relative) effective sample size, `n_eff` and `r_eff`.
+ `$log_weights`: the log PSIS weights.

```{r}
names(loo_sleep_measure)
```

**Plot** 
The following plot compares the in-sample and LOO scores for
three measures: the log score, the RPS, and the squared error. Each point
is one observation. The x-axis shows the in-sample value, and the y-axis
the LOO value. The color shows the Pareto $\hat k$. We do not show `mlpd`
and `r2`. Their pointwise values are the same as those of `elpd` and `rmse`.

```{r loo-plot, echo=FALSE}
pw_measures <- c(
  elpd = "log score (higher is better)",
  rps  = "RPS (lower is better)",
  rmse = "squared error (lower is better)"
)

df_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pw_measures), function(m) data.frame(
  measure  = pw_measures[[m]],
  insample = insample_sleep$pointwise[, m],
  loo      = loo_sleep_measure$pointwise[, paste0(m, "_loo")],
  pareto_k = loo_sleep_measure$diagnostics$pareto_k
)))

ggplot(df_all, aes(insample, loo, color = pareto_k)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "pointwise in-sample value",
       y = "pointwise LOO value",
       color = "Pareto k") +
  geom_blank(aes(x = loo, y = insample))
```

The log score is a utility (higher is better). The RPS and the squared error
are losses (lower is better). Thus, an observation that is harder to predict
when it is left out lies below the diagonal for the log score, but above the
diagonal for the RPS and the squared error. The farther a point lies from the
diagonal, the more the observation influences the posterior. Such
observations often have a high Pareto $\hat k$. The color lets you check
whether an influential observation moves away from the diagonal for all
measures or only for some.

### K-fold {#k-fold}
Next, we focus on K-fold cross-validation. The data are split into $K$ folds.
The model is fit once for each fold, without the observations in that fold.
This needs $K$ fits, not $n$.

**Implementation**
**loo** does not refit the model. We first compute the K-fold object using
`brms::kfold()`. Set `save_fits = TRUE`. Without the fits,
`brms::kfold_predict()` cannot compute the held-out draws:
`method = "predict"` gives `ypred`, and `method = "fitted"` gives `mupred`.

```{r kfold, results="hide"}
set.seed(SEED)
kfold_sleep <- brms::kfold(fit_full, K = 5, save_fits = TRUE)
ypred_kfold <- brms::kfold_predict(kfold_sleep, method = "predict")$yrep
mupred_kfold <- brms::kfold_predict(kfold_sleep, method = "fitted")$yrep
```

We then pass the K-fold object to `kfold_pred_measure()`. Otherwise, the input
structure is the same as for the in-sample evaluation.

```{r kfold-measures}
kfold_sleep_measure <- kfold_pred_measure(
  y = y,
  ypred = ypred_kfold,
  mupred = mupred_kfold,
  kfold = kfold_sleep,
  measures = measures
)
kfold_sleep_measure
```

**Result**
The rows in the result object now have the suffix `_kfold`.
The measure `elpd` also adds `p_kfold`, the difference between the in-sample
and the K-fold log score.

The output structure of the `kfold_pred_measure` class takes the attributes
`K`, `folds`, `fold_type`, `joint`, `yhash`, and `model_name` from the `kfold`
object. It has `$diagnostics` only when the `kfold` object has them. Recent
versions of `brms::kfold()` do. K-fold uses no importance weights, so there is
no `$log_weights` component.

```{r}
names(kfold_sleep_measure)
```

**Plot**
The following plot has the same layout as the PSIS-LOO plot. The y-axis now
shows the K-fold value. The color shows the fold of each observation.

```{r kfold-plot, echo=FALSE}
df_kfold <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pw_measures), function(m) data.frame(
  measure  = pw_measures[[m]],
  insample = insample_sleep$pointwise[, m],
  kfold    = kfold_sleep_measure$pointwise[, paste0(m, "_kfold")],
  fold     = factor(attr(kfold_sleep_measure, "folds"))
)))

ggplot(df_kfold, aes(insample, kfold, color = fold)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "pointwise in-sample value",
       y = "pointwise K-fold value",
       color = "fold") +
  geom_blank(aes(x = kfold, y = insample))
```

The direction of the diagonal is the same as in the PSIS-LOO plot. With
$K = 5$, each fit uses about 80% of the data. Thus K-fold and PSIS-LOO answer a
similar question. Each K-fold fit has less data than a LOO fit, so the K-fold
estimates are often slightly worse. Use K-fold when PSIS-LOO shows many high
Pareto $\hat k$ values.

`brms::kfold()` also accepts `folds = "grouped"` with `group = "Subject"`. Then
each fold holds out whole subjects, and the predictive question changes to new
subjects.

### Test data {#test-data}
Finally, we focus on the test data scheme. The data are split once into a
training set and a test set. The model is fit only to the training set. It then
predicts the test set, which it did not see. For the current example, we hold out
five subjects. This gives 40 test observations.

This scheme needs no importance weights and no refits. It needs one fit to the
training data.

**Implementation**
We compute the draws of `fit_train` at `test_data` with `newdata`. Pass the log
densities of the test observations as `ylp_test`, not as `ylp`. The measures
`elpd`, `mlpd`, and `ic` need `ylp_test`.

```{r test}
ypred_test <- brms::posterior_predict(fit_train, newdata = test_data)
mupred_test <- brms::posterior_epred(fit_train, newdata = test_data)
ylp_test <- brms::log_lik(fit_train, newdata = test_data)

test_sleep_measure <- test_pred_measure(
  y = test_data$y,
  ypred = ypred_test,
  mupred = mupred_test,
  ylp_test = ylp_test,
  measures = measures
)
test_sleep_measure
```

**Result**
The rows in the result object now have the suffix `_test`. The attribute
`dims` gives the size of the test set, 40 observations, not the size of the
training set. The output has only `$estimates` and `$pointwise`.

```{r}
names(test_sleep_measure)
```

**Plot**
The test observations are not in the training data. Thus there is no in-sample
value. The following plot shows the pointwise test values on the y-axis for
each of the five test subjects on the x-axis.

```{r test-plot, echo=FALSE}
df_test <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pw_measures), function(m) data.frame(
  measure = pw_measures[[m]],
  subject = test_data$Subject,
  test    = test_sleep_measure$pointwise[, paste0(m, "_test")]
)))

ggplot(df_test, aes(subject, test, color = subject)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, seed = SEED)) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "test subject", y = "pointwise test value") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The test set holds five subjects that the model did not see. The plot shows whether
one subject controls the estimate. The test set is small, so the standard errors
are larger than in the other schemes. A different split can give
a different estimate.

## Comparison of predictive schemes {#compare-predictive-schemes}
All four schemes use the same model and the same measures. They differ in the
predictive question. The plot shows the estimate and $\pm 1$ standard error
for each scheme and measure.

`elpd` is a sum over the evaluation data (Vehtari et al., 2026, Eq. 2.7). The
test set has 40 observations, and the other schemes have 144. Thus do not
compare the `elpd` of the test data with the other schemes. Use `mlpd` for
this comparison.

```{r scheme-overview, echo=FALSE}
results <- list(
  "in-sample" = insample_sleep$estimates,
  "PSIS-LOO"  = loo_sleep_measure$estimates,
  "K-fold"    = kfold_sleep_measure$estimates,
  "test data" = test_sleep_measure$estimates
)
suffix <- c("in-sample" = "", "PSIS-LOO" = "_loo", "K-fold" = "_kfold",
            "test data" = "_test")
direction <- c(elpd = "higher", mlpd = "higher", rps = "lower",
               rmse = "lower", r2 = "higher")

df_est <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(results), function(s) {
  est <- results[[s]][paste0(measures, suffix[[s]]), , drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(
    scheme   = s,
    measure  = paste0(measures, " (", direction[measures], " is better)"),
    estimate = est[, "Estimate"],
    se       = est[, "SE"]
  )
}))

df_est$scheme <- factor(df_est$scheme, levels = rev(names(results)))
df_est$measure <- factor(df_est$measure, levels = unique(df_est$measure))

ggplot(df_est, aes(estimate, scheme, color = scheme)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = estimate - se, xmax = estimate + se),
                 linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("in-sample" = "grey50", "PSIS-LOO" = "#0072B2",
               "K-fold" = "#009E73", "test data" = "#D55E00"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, ncol = 3, nrow = 2, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "estimate ± 1 SE", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "grey70", fill = NA),
        panel.spacing.y = unit(1, "lines"),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey92", color = "grey70"),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
```

In-sample, PSIS-LOO, and K-fold score the same 144 observations. The
in-sample estimate is the most optimistic, because the model has seen each
$y_i$. PSIS-LOO and K-fold ask a similar question, so their estimates are
close. The test data score five new subjects. The interval of the test data is
wider, because the test set has only 40 observations. One split is noisy. A
different split can move the estimate to the other side of PSIS-LOO.

## Add measures to an existing result {#add-measures}

Besides the four scheme functions, the family has `pred_measure()`.
This function adds measures to an object of class `pred_measure`. It takes the
predictive scheme from the result, for example `kfold`, and adds new measures to
the result object. If a requested measure is already stored, `pred_measure()`
warns and skips it.

For example, we first compute only `elpd` with PSIS-LOO.

```{r}
loo_elpd <- loo_pred_measure(loo = loo_sleep, save_psis = TRUE)
loo_elpd
```

To add further measures to the output, we can now use `pred_measure()` and
provide the additional measures with their required input. Additionally, we
pass the initially computed result object (here: `loo_elpd`).

```{r add-measures}
pred_measure(
  y = y,
  mupred = mupred,
  predperf = loo_elpd,
  measures = c("mae", "rmse")
)
```

## Custom measures {#custom-measures}

The argument `measures` also accepts functions. Use them to define custom
measures. A custom function must follow three rules:

+ **Arguments.** Name the arguments from `y`, `ypred`, `mupred`, `ylp`, and
  `log_weights`. **loo** maps the inputs by these names.
+ **Weights.** `log_weights` holds the PSIS weights for PSIS-LOO. In the other
  schemes it is `NULL`. A function that ignores `log_weights` gives in-sample
  values under PSIS-LOO.
+ **Return value.** Return a list with `estimate`, `se`, and `pointwise`.

After you construct the custom function, wrap it in
`custom_measure()`, which sets the name, whether the measure is a loss (lower is
better) or a utility, and how `model_compare()` computes the standard error of a
difference (`se_diff_fun`). The default is a utility (higher is better). If you do not give
`se_diff_fun`, `model_compare()` reports an `NA` standard error.

**Example.** The coverage of the central 90% predictive interval is the
proportion of observations inside that interval. For a calibrated model, it is
close to 0.9. Observation $i$ is inside the interval when its probability
integral transform lies between 0.05 and 0.95:

$$
\text{pit}_i = \sum_{s=1}^S w_i^s\, \mathbb{1}\{\tilde y_i^s \le y_i\},
\qquad
\text{cover}_i = \mathbb{1}\{0.05 < \text{pit}_i \le 0.95\} .
$$

```{r custom-function}
coverage <- function(y, ypred, log_weights = NULL, prob = 0.9) {
  if (is.null(log_weights)) {
    log_weights <- matrix(-log(nrow(ypred)), nrow(ypred), ncol(ypred))
  }
  w <- exp(sweep(log_weights, 2, matrixStats::colLogSumExps(log_weights)))
  pit <- colSums(w * sweep(ypred, 2, y, "<="))
  alpha <- 1 - prob
  cover_i <- as.numeric(pit > alpha / 2 & pit <= 1 - alpha / 2)
  list(
    estimate = mean(cover_i),
    se = sqrt(var(cover_i) / length(cover_i)),
    pointwise = cover_i
  )
}
```

The same function works in every scheme:

```{r custom-measures}
cover90 <- custom_measure(coverage, name = "cover90", se_diff_fun = "mean")

insample_pred_measure(
  y = y,
  ypred = ypred,
  measures = list("rps", cover90 = cover90)
)

loo_pred_measure(
  loo = loo_sleep,
  y = y,
  ypred = ypred,
  measures = list("rps", cover90 = cover90)
)
```
